input: The thickness of the wall of the absorber, once the corrosion allowance has been added on top of the thickness required by the pressure calculation, works out at 90 mm, and it is worth appreciating that the margin contained in this figure is provided by the allowance rather than by the pressure calculation itself. The corrosion allowance is, of course, gradually consumed over the life of the vessel, which means that the thickness present at commissioning is not the thickness the pressure case sees late in the inspection interval. Turning to the gasket that seals the same joint, the two candidate materials have been compared on the basis of temperature limit alone. One of the two materials is rated to a significantly higher temperature than the other, and it is the higher-rated material that is preferred, because the joint is exposed to the full operating temperature of the absorber, so that a gasket operating right at the limit of its rating would be left with no margin to accommodate any excursion. It should be emphasised that temperature limit is the only ground on which the two materials are being compared here; sealing behaviour under pressure belongs to the flange calculation, where the $\Delta P$ across the joint appears as a load case rather than as a ground for selection. Circulation against which the absorber operates is established by the lean solvent pump, and its NPSH margin is derived from the suction condition at the operating level, a condition that neither the wall thickness nor the gasket selection has any bearing upon. An open interaction between the two choices remains, in that a gasket which creeps at temperature relaxes the bolt load that the wall thickness calculation takes for granted, and the rate of that relaxation at the operating temperature is the quantity the comparison still has to establish.
